n: Now the Lord addresses the priests, Aaron’s sons. Touching a corpse caused ritual uncleanness, so priests were generally to avoid funerals.

f.g: Made ritually unclean by contact with a dead body.

n: An exception: a priest may become unclean to mourn his closest relatives—parents, children, and brother. God honored family grief.

f.g: kin = relatives

n: He may also mourn an unmarried sister who still lived under his family’s care.

f.g: nigh = near, close

n: But as a leader he must not defile himself for others, such as relatives by marriage.

f.g: A leader; possibly “as a husband,” meaning for in-laws. The Hebrew is uncertain.

n: Priests must not shave their heads, trim their beards, or cut their skin—mourning customs of pagan neighbors.
Because they offer “the bread of their God”—the sacrifices—priests must be holy. Their role represented God to the people.

f.g: A term for the offerings, pictured as food set before God.

n: A priest must not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman, since his household reflected his sacred role.

f.g: Here, a woman who has been defiled or dishonored.
put away = divorced

n: Israel must treat the priest as holy because of his service, and God, who is holy, is the one who sanctifies them all.
A priest’s daughter who becomes a prostitute brings disgrace on her father; the penalty is death. The priest’s family was held to a higher standard.

f.g: Committing prostitution or sexual immorality.

n: The high priest, anointed and wearing the holy garments, has stricter rules. He must not show mourning by uncovering his head or tearing his clothes.

f.g: Tear one’s garments, a common sign of grief.

n: He may not approach any dead body—not even for his own parents. His duty to the living God came first.

f.w: go in to any dead body

n: He must not leave the sanctuary to mourn, because the holy anointing oil is like a crown upon him.

f.g: The anointing marked him as consecrated, like a crown marks a king.

n: The high priest must marry a virgin.
He may not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, but only a young woman from Israel.

f.g: harlot = prostitute

n: This protected the purity of the high priestly line, which God Himself sanctified.

f.g: offspring, descendants

n: A new instruction is given to Moses.
Descendants of Aaron with a physical defect may not offer sacrifices. Like the animals offered, the officiant was to be “without blemish”—a picture of perfection pointing to Christ.

f.g: A physical defect.

n: Examples include blindness, lameness, or a disfigured face or limb.

f.g: Some disfigurement of the face; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Having a deformed or extra limb.

n: Also an injured foot or hand.

f.g: With a crippled foot.

n: Also a hunched back, short stature, eye defects, skin diseases, or damaged reproductive organs.

f.g: Hunchbacked.
Having a skin disease or rash, not the vitamin disease.
testicles

n: These men may not serve at the altar. The rule concerned outward symbolism in worship, not a person’s worth before God.
Yet they still eat the holy food and keep their priestly share. They remain fully part of the priestly family.

f.w: most holy, and of the holy
f.g: Two classes of priestly food from the offerings.

n: Only service at the veil and altar is restricted. God’s concern was the visible symbolism of His sanctuary.
Moses passes the instructions on to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel—priestly rules were public knowledge.
